case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 18 U.S.C. 922(g)(3), which prohibits firearm possession by unlawful drug users or addicts, violates the Second Amendment as applied to respondent Ali Danial Hemani.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. 922(g)(3) — prohibiting possession of firearms by any person who 'is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance,' evaluated against the Second Amendment of the United States Constitution, with the analytical framework established in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that Section 922(g)(3) is constitutionally valid because: (1) historical analogues exist — particularly laws disarming intoxicated individuals and the mentally ill — that are sufficiently analogous to justify disarming habitual unlawful drug users; (2) the Fifth Circuit's invalidation of most applications of the statute created a clear and deepening circuit conflict requiring Supreme Court resolution; (3) the statute serves a compelling public safety interest affecting hundreds of prosecutions annually; and (4) individuals who habitually use unlawful drugs present dangers analogous to those historically excluded from Second Amendment protections, regardless of whether they are actively under the influence at the precise moment of firearm possession.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Hemani argues that Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied because: (1) under the Bruen historical-tradition framework, the government cannot identify sufficiently analogous historical laws that disarmed sober individuals merely because they habitually used intoxicants; (2) the statute is overbroad in sweeping in individuals who are not actively intoxicated or impaired at the time of possession; (3) the mere status of being an unlawful drug user, absent present intoxication or demonstrated dangerousness, does not historically justify categorical disarmament; and (4) the Bruen framework requires a closer historical fit than the government's proposed analogues provide.
key_precedents: New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen (2022) — established the historical-tradition test for Second Amendment challenges
District of Columbia v. Heller (2008) — foundational Second Amendment ruling recognizing individual right to bear arms
McDonald v. City of Chicago (2010) — incorporated Second Amendment against the states
United States v. Harris, No. 21-3031, 2025 WL 1922605 (3d Cir. July 14, 2025) — deepened circuit split on Section 922(g)(3)'s constitutionality
United States v. Rahimi (2024) — Supreme Court addressed Second Amendment historical-analogue methodology post-Bruen
United States v. Hill, 703 F. Supp. 3d 729 (E.D. Va. 2023), aff'd, 2025 WL 314159 (4th Cir. Jan. 28, 2025) — district court critique of Bruen framework's workability and historical-record limitations
Seventh Circuit precedent upholding Section 922(g)(3) based on historical laws disarming the intoxicated and mentally ill
William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England (10th ed. 1787) — cited as historical authority on English common law traditions regarding arms and public safety

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's argument that the historical analogues address *present* impairment rather than status-based disarmament of sober individuals remains the most serious challenge, and I want to engage it directly: he is correct that the 'how' of historical intoxication laws was temporary restraint during dangerous episodes, not categorical prohibition. However, I am persuaded that this framing conflates the 'how' with the 'why' — Rahimi teaches that the 'how' need not be identical, only relevantly similar, and a conditional, reversible prohibition on habitual users is a lesser restriction than civil commitment or imprisonment, which the historical record does support. Justice Thomas's demand for a founding-era statute categorically disarming habitual drunkards by status alone sets precisely the 'historical twin' standard that Rahimi explicitly rejected. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion to Justice Barrett with instructions to write narrowly on as-applied grounds, emphasizing that today's holding reaches only habitual users whose pattern of conduct reflects the chronic judgment impairment the historical tradition targeted, explicitly preserving robust as-applied challenges for individuals at the margins — this framing should hold our 7-justice coalition while giving Justice Gorsuch's legitimate concerns their due weight in limiting the opinion's reach.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that Rahimi rejected the 'historical twin' requirement and permits analogical reasoning at a principled level of generality is the most sophisticated challenge to my position, but it ultimately cannot bear the weight placed upon it: Rahimi's analogical flexibility was exercised in a case involving an active judicial finding of individualized dangerousness, and the Court's language about 'relevantly similar' was not a license to aggregate disparate historical practices — imprisonment of drunkards, surety laws, intoxication restrictions — into a composite tradition that no single founding-era legislature actually enacted. Justice Alito's argument that the statute is 'lesser' than historical confinement powers fails on its own logic, as Justice Gorsuch correctly identifies: a permanent status-based federal prohibition on a sober individual is not a lesser version of temporary restraint during active intoxication — it is a categorically different regulatory mechanism targeting a categorically different condition. The majority's as-applied framing, endorsed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett, actually concedes my core point: if the statute requires as-applied narrowing to survive, that is because its categorical text sweeps beyond what the historical tradition supports, and the proper remedy is to hold the statute unconstitutional as applied to Hemani rather than to rewrite it through judicial construction. I maintain my position for the Respondent because the Bruen methodology I articulated requires more than analogical aggregation — it requires that the government demonstrate a historical tradition of the specific regulatory burden imposed, and no such tradition of status-based disarmament of sober habitual users exists in the founding-era record.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious challenge by arguing that founding-era analogues targeted presently dangerous or actively intoxicated persons rather than imposing categorical status-based prohibitions on sober individuals — but this argument proves too much, because Rahimi itself upheld a categorical prohibition on domestic violence restraining order subjects who were not necessarily actively dangerous at every moment of possession. The 'why' of historical intoxicant disarmament laws was not merely to prevent harm during active impairment but to address the class of persons whose habitual relationship with intoxicants made them chronically unreliable custodians of deadly weapons — precisely the same regulatory logic animating Section 922(g)(3). Justice Gorsuch's concern about individualized adjudication is undercut by the fact that Rahimi endorsed categorical disarmament without requiring case-by-case dangerousness findings, and the statute's conditional nature — rights restored upon cessation of habitual use — aligns with the 'lesser restriction' logic I find persuasive. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that we should write narrowly, confining our holding to habitual users whose pattern of conduct creates the chronic impairment the historical tradition addressed, while preserving as-applied challenges for marginal cases.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's argument that the historical analogues address *present* impairment rather than status-based prohibition remains the most intellectually honest challenge, and I want to engage it directly: he is correct that the 'how' of historical intoxication laws was typically temporary restraint during dangerous episodes, not categorical prohibition. However, I think he draws the wrong conclusion from this asymmetry. The 'lesser includes the greater' logic cuts both ways — if the founding generation accepted imprisonment of habitual drunkards as a legitimate response to chronic impairment, then a conditional, reversible firearms prohibition is a lesser intrusion on liberty targeting the same chronic judgment impairment, not a categorically different mechanism. Justice Thomas's demand for a statute that precisely mirrors Section 922(g)(3) is exactly the 'historical twin' requirement Rahimi rejected, and while I share Justice Jackson's concern — rooted in my own experience with how status-based prohibitions sweep broadly — the as-applied posture here, involving a documented habitual user, means we can uphold this conviction while preserving robust as-applied challenges for individuals whose circumstances fall outside the historical tradition's core justification.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's argument that the 'why' of historical intoxication laws was preventing imminent danger from present impairment — not punishing a behavioral pattern — and that the 'how' was temporary restraint rather than categorical prohibition, remains the most analytically precise challenge to my position. But I think this framing, while rigorous, ultimately demands more historical specificity than Rahimi permits: the civil commitment and surety traditions Justice Barrett identifies reflect founding-era recognition that chronic behavioral patterns — not just episodic episodes — could justify prospective restraint on dangerous instrumentalities, which is the relevant analogical principle. Justice Gorsuch is correct that we cannot simply invoke 'greater includes the lesser' to transform a temporary restraint on active intoxication into a categorical status-based prohibition, and this is precisely why I continue to insist that the holding must be cabined to the as-applied challenge before us, where Hemani's habitual use pattern — not mere status — provides the nexus to the historical tradition's core concern. The 7-2 tally does not move me to increase my confidence beyond what the legal merits warrant, and I would write separately to emphasize that the as-applied limitation is not a concession but a constitutional necessity that preserves the statute's validity only within its historically grounded core.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett's as-applied framing is the most sophisticated attempt to bridge the historical gap, and I genuinely respect her effort to cabin the holding narrowly — but it does not resolve my core methodological objection. The 'why and how' test from Rahimi requires that both prongs be satisfied, and even on an as-applied basis, the government has not demonstrated that Hemani was actively impaired or presently dangerous at the moment of possession, which is precisely what the historical analogues actually required. Justice Kavanaugh's invocation of Rahimi's rejection of the 'historical twin' requirement is well-taken, but Rahimi involved an active judicial finding of individual dangerousness through a civil protective order — a procedural predicate that provided the individualized nexus the historical tradition demanded — whereas Section 922(g)(3) imposes categorical disarmament based on a behavioral status determination made without any contemporaneous judicial finding of present dangerousness. The majority's collective reliance on surety laws and civil commitment traditions as analogues for the 'how' prong actually undermines their position: those mechanisms were precisely calibrated, individualized proceedings — not categorical status-based prohibitions — which confirms that the founding generation understood the 'how' of restricting dangerous persons to require individualized adjudication rather than legislative categorization by status alone.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's argument that the 'why' of historical intoxication laws was preventing imminent danger from present impairment — not punishing a behavioral pattern — and that the 'how' was temporary restraint during the dangerous episode remains the most serious challenge to my position. However, I find it ultimately unpersuasive for the same reason I find Justice Thomas's similar argument unpersuasive: Rahimi itself upheld a status-based categorical prohibition on persons subject to domestic violence restraining orders, who were not necessarily actively dangerous at every moment of possession, and the Court explicitly rejected the demand for a near-identical historical twin. Justice Gorsuch's framing that a status-based prohibition is 'categorically different' from temporary restraint during active impairment proves too much — by that logic, Rahimi itself would have come out differently, since a restraining order subject is not actively threatening at every moment of firearm possession. I remain persuaded by the collective weight of the historical tradition — intoxication laws, surety laws, civil commitment practices — and by the institutional considerations Justice Roberts emphasizes: writing narrowly on as-applied grounds resolves the circuit conflict while preserving robust as-applied challenges for individuals whose circumstances fall outside the historical tradition's core, which adequately addresses the legitimate concerns Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas raise about categorical status-based disarmament.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's argument that the 'why' and 'how' of historical intoxication laws targeted present impairment rather than status-based prohibition remains the most intellectually serious challenge, and I want to engage it directly: he is correct that the historical analogues do not map perfectly, but Rahimi itself involved a status-based restriction — being subject to a civil protective order — where the subject was not necessarily actively dangerous at every moment of possession, yet the Court upheld it. The critical move in my analysis is that 'habitual user' is not merely a status label but a description of a pattern of conduct that creates chronic, foreseeable impairment of judgment — the same chronic unreliability that founding-era legislatures addressed through surety laws and civil commitment, which were themselves prospective and status-adjacent rather than tied to present dangerousness at the moment of restraint. Justice Thomas's demand for a founding-era statute that categorically stripped arms from habitual drunkards by status alone sets the historical-twin bar that Rahimi explicitly rejected, and while I acknowledge the analogues are imperfect, the 'relevantly similar' standard at an appropriate level of generality is satisfied by the constellation of historical practices targeting chronic impairment combined with dangerous instrumentalities. I maintain my position for the Petitioner on the narrow as-applied grounds Justice Roberts has articulated, while acknowledging that Justice Gorsuch's concerns about the statute's categorical sweep counsel strongly against any facial validation and in favor of preserving robust as-applied challenges.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's argument remains the most intellectually challenging to my position — his point that the historical 'why' was preventing imminent danger from present impairment, not punishing a behavioral pattern, and that the 'how' was temporary restraint rather than categorical prohibition, identifies a genuine methodological tension that I cannot fully dismiss. However, I find it ultimately unpersuasive for two reasons rooted in my reading of Rahimi: first, Rahimi upheld disarmament of a domestic violence restraining order subject who was not actively dangerous at every moment of possession, demonstrating that status-based restrictions with individualized predicate findings can satisfy the historical tradition even without present impairment; and second, the historical practice of civilly committing habitual drunkards — which Rahimi recognized as supporting 'lesser restriction' logic — reflects a judgment about chronic behavioral patterns, not merely episodic incapacity. My public defender background makes me genuinely sympathetic to Justice Gorsuch's concern that categorical status-based prohibitions sweep in individuals who pose no genuine danger, which is precisely why I insist that today's holding must be confined to the as-applied challenge involving a habitual user whose pattern of conduct reflects the chronic judgment impairment the historical tradition targeted, leaving robust space for future as-applied challenges by individuals whose circumstances fall outside that core.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Rahimi's clarification of Bruen's methodology, the government need not produce a precise historical twin but rather demonstrate that Section 922(g)(3) fits within a broader historical tradition of disarming individuals whose condition renders them dangerous — a tradition evidenced by colonial and founding-era laws restricting intoxicated persons from bearing arms and categorical disarmament of those deemed mentally unfit. Writing narrowly, I would hold only that habitual unlawful drug users, as a class, fall within this historical tradition because their pattern of conduct — not merely momentary intoxication — creates the kind of ongoing danger that historical legislatures recognized as justifying disarmament, analogous to the 'why' and 'how' analysis Rahimi endorsed. I would not reach the broader question of whether any marijuana user or someone with a remote history of drug use falls within the statute's reach, preserving as-applied challenges for individuals who can demonstrate their circumstances fall outside this historical tradition. This narrow ruling resolves the deepening circuit conflict while respecting institutional legitimacy by avoiding an unnecessarily sweeping constitutional pronouncement that could destabilize hundreds of related prosecutions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Applying the Bruen historical-tradition framework rigorously, the government bears the burden of demonstrating that Section 922(g)(3)'s categorical status-based disarmament of habitual drug users is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation, and that burden has not been met as applied to Hemani. The government's proffered analogues — vagrancy laws, civil commitment statutes, and surety laws — do not constitute laws that actually disarmed individuals based on habitual intoxicant use absent present dangerousness or active impairment; as the research confirms, petitioner cites no founding-era statute that categorically stripped arms rights from habitual drunkards merely by virtue of that status. While Rahimi (2024) confirmed that historical analogues need not be identical twins to modern regulations, it still requires that the 'why and how' of the historical restriction be relevantly similar, and laws targeting presently dangerous or actively intoxicated persons are categorically distinct from a permanent status-based prohibition on a sober individual possessing firearms. As I emphasized in my Bruen concurrence, the Second Amendment's text protects 'the people,' and departures from that protection require genuine historical grounding, not analogical extrapolation from laws that addressed different harms through different means.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutionally valid under the Bruen historical-tradition framework because there exists a deeply rooted American tradition of temporarily disarming individuals whose judgment and self-control are compromised by intoxicants, and Rahimi confirmed that historical analogues need not be 'twins' but must share a comparable 'why' and 'how.' The historical tradition of disarming habitual drunkards — including laws permitting imprisonment of such individuals, which Rahimi recognized as supporting the 'lesser restriction' of temporary disarmament — provides a sufficiently analogous basis for disarming habitual unlawful drug users, who present comparable dangers to public safety. The statute's restriction is appropriately limited and temporary, as a person regains Second Amendment rights upon ceasing habitual drug use, and as I noted in my Rehaif dissent, Section 922(g) 'probably does more to combat gun violence than any other federal law,' reflecting Congress's well-founded judgment that drugs and guns are a dangerous combination. Respondent's demand for a near-perfect historical twin would render Bruen's framework unworkable and would improperly discount the practical public safety consequences of invalidating hundreds of prosecutions annually under a statute targeting a class of individuals whose habitual illegal conduct demonstrably impairs the responsible exercise of Second Amendment rights.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: While I have deep reservations about the Bruen framework's rigid historical-analogue methodology — which I believe improperly constrains legislatures from addressing modern public safety crises — I am persuaded that Section 922(g)(3) survives constitutional scrutiny under Rahimi's more flexible reading of historical tradition. As Rahimi clarified, the Second Amendment inquiry asks whether a modern regulation is 'relevantly similar' to historical analogues in its 'why' and 'how,' not whether it is a precise historical twin; founding-era laws imprisoning habitual drunkards, imposing surety bonds on those posing dangers, and restricting arms near intoxicated persons collectively establish a tradition of disarming individuals whose habitual conduct creates foreseeable risks to public safety. The government's analogy is not merely status-based in a vacuum — habitual unlawful drug use, like habitual drunkenness at the founding, reflects a pattern of conduct that historically justified heightened regulation of dangerous instrumentalities, and Rahimi's 'greater includes the lesser' logic supports that if imprisonment of habitual drunkards was permissible, temporary disarmament of habitual drug users is as well. I write separately to emphasize that this holding should be construed narrowly, that as-applied challenges remain available to individuals who can demonstrate their use does not create the dangerousness the statute targets, and that the Bruen framework's historical fetishism continues to threaten sensible gun regulations protecting vulnerable communities.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Rahimi's 'relevantly similar' standard, the historical tradition of disarming intoxicated individuals provides a sufficiently analogous basis for Section 922(g)(3), because the 'why' — preventing firearms from reaching those whose judgment and impulse control are compromised by substance use — maps onto the same regulatory principle, even if the 'how' differs between momentary intoxication and habitual use. Rahimi confirmed that Bruen does not demand a 'historical twin' but rather a 'historical analogue,' and the longstanding legislative authority to categorically disarm those who pose heightened danger to the community supports Congress's judgment that habitual unlawful drug users present precisely that risk. While I share some concern about the statute's breadth — particularly its application to individuals who are sober at the moment of possession — the as-applied challenge here does not require us to invalidate the statute wholesale, and a narrowing construction tethering the prohibition to demonstrated habitual use rather than mere experimental contact preserves the statute's core public safety function while respecting Second Amendment limits. The workability concerns raised by courts like the Fourth Circuit about Bruen's historical methodology are real, but Rahimi's pragmatic recalibration of that framework gives us sufficient tools to uphold this provision without rendering the Second Amendment's protections illusory.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Applying Bruen's historical-tradition methodology rigorously, the government's proposed analogues — laws targeting actively intoxicated persons, vagrancy statutes, and civil commitment proceedings — do not provide a sufficiently close historical fit to justify the categorical, status-based disarmament of sober individuals who merely have a history of unlawful drug use. The 'why' and 'how' inquiry from Rahimi demands that analogues be relevantly similar in both burden and justification: historical laws disarming drunkards during intervals of sobriety were narrow, localized, and typically required individualized adjudication, not a blanket federal prohibition triggered by mere status. While Rahimi's dangerousness principle is real, it cannot be stretched into a regulatory blank check that permits Congress to disarm entire categories of 'the people' based on behavioral status without an individualized finding of present dangerousness — otherwise Bruen's historical-tradition test loses all limiting force. As applied to Hemani, who was not shown to be actively intoxicated or imminently dangerous at the time of possession, Section 922(g)(3) sweeps too broadly beyond what founding-era tradition can support.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Rahimi's 'relevantly similar' standard, the government need not identify a historical twin but rather a historical analogue that shares the same 'why' and 'how' of disarmament — and the deeply rooted tradition of temporarily disarming intoxicated individuals, combined with historical laws addressing the mentally ill and those deemed dangerous to public order, provides sufficient analogical support for Section 922(g)(3) as applied to habitual unlawful drug users. As Rahimi clarified, Bruen does not demand a 'historical twin' but permits analogical reasoning from established traditions, and the tradition of disarming those whose judgment and self-control are chronically impaired by intoxicants is well-documented in English and early American law, including Blackstone's commentaries. The statute's temporary and conditional nature — a person regains firearm rights upon cessation of habitual use — further aligns with the historical pattern of status-based, reversible disarmament rather than permanent categorical exclusion, making it more constitutionally defensible than a lifetime ban. While I share some concern about the statute's breadth and the workability challenges the Fourth Circuit identified with the Bruen framework, institutional considerations counsel upholding a federal statute with significant public safety implications where a plausible historical tradition exists, consistent with the Court's approach in Rahimi.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying Rahimi's clarification that Bruen requires 'relevantly similar' rather than identical historical analogues, the historical tradition of disarming intoxicated individuals and those deemed dangerous to the public order provides a sufficiently analogous foundation for Section 922(g)(3)'s categorical prohibition on habitual unlawful drug users. Rahimi confirmed that courts must assess the 'why' and 'how' of historical regulations at a principled level of generality — the 'why' being the prevention of harm from those whose judgment and self-control are chronically compromised, and the 'how' being categorical status-based disarmament — both of which are satisfied here by the analogy to historical intoxication and mental incapacity laws documented in Blackstone and early American statutes. While I share some of the respondent's concern that the statute as written sweeps broadly and could reach individuals who pose no present danger, the as-applied challenge here involves a habitual user whose pattern of unlawful drug use is precisely the chronic impairment of judgment that historical disarmament traditions targeted, distinguishing this case from a mere occasional or remote past user. I would uphold the statute as applied to Hemani while reserving judgment on whether the statute's full breadth survives constitutional scrutiny in all applications, consistent with the Court's incremental, case-by-case methodology endorsed in Rahimi.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Rahimi's 'relevantly similar' standard, the historical tradition of temporarily disarming intoxicated individuals provides a sufficiently analogous basis for Section 922(g)(3)'s disarmament of habitual unlawful drug users, as both share the same 'why' — preventing the dangers posed by impaired judgment combined with deadly weapons — and a comparable 'how' — temporary, status-based restrictions that lift upon cessation of the dangerous conduct. While I share concerns about the statute's breadth and the Bruen framework's workability as critiqued in Hill, Rahimi instructs that historical analogues need not be 'twins' but must be 'relevantly similar,' and the longstanding recognition that 'drugs and guns are a dangerous combination,' Smith v. United States, 508 U.S. 223 (1993), supports the government's position that habitual unlawful drug use presents dangers analogous to chronic intoxication. My background as a public defender gives me serious pause about status-based categorical disarmament and the overbreadth concerns Hemani raises — particularly for individuals not actively impaired at the moment of possession — but the as-applied challenge here, combined with the circuit conflict and public safety stakes affecting hundreds of prosecutions, counsels in favor of upholding the statute while leaving room for narrower as-applied challenges in future cases where the nexus to dangerousness is weaker.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 18 U.S.C. 922(g)(3), which prohibits firearm possession by unlawful drug users or addicts, violates the Second Amendment as applied to respondent Ali Danial Hemani.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. 922(g)(3) — prohibiting firearm possession by any person who 'is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance,' evaluated against the Second Amendment to the United States Constitution, with the constitutional analysis framework established in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that Section 922(g)(3) is constitutionally valid because: (1) historical tradition supports disarming individuals who pose heightened dangers to public safety, including those who are intoxicated or mentally impaired; (2) historical analogues — such as laws prohibiting firearm possession by intoxicated individuals and the mentally ill — are sufficiently similar in justification and burden to support the statute's constitutionality; (3) the Fifth Circuit's invalidation of most applications of the statute created a clear and deepening circuit conflict (now joined by the Third Circuit in United States v. Harris) that demands Supreme Court resolution; and (4) the ruling below threatens hundreds of federal prosecutions annually, undermining an important public safety tool.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent Hemani argues that Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied because: (1) under the Bruen historical-tradition framework, the government cannot identify sufficiently analogous historical laws that disarmed individuals merely for being habitual drug users when not actively under the influence at the time of firearm possession; (2) the statute is overbroad in that it sweeps in individuals who may not be presently impaired or dangerous at the moment of possession; (3) the Fifth Circuit correctly found that the government failed to meet its burden of demonstrating a historical tradition of disarming this category of persons; and (4) the Bruen framework, properly applied, does not permit the government to extend historical intoxication-based analogues to cover all habitual unlawful drug users regardless of their actual state at the time of possession.

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has achieved remarkable unanimity, and I am satisfied that the collective reasoning — particularly Justice Gorsuch's clarification that Rahimi's surety law analysis already endorsed status-based disarmament tied to demonstrated dangerousness rather than requiring proof of active impairment at the moment of possession — directly answers the Fifth Circuit's core methodological error without requiring us to reach broader questions. Justice Thomas's methodological concern about Rahimi's analogical approach potentially untethering analysis from original public meaning is the most intellectually serious challenge raised in conference, but I am persuaded that on these specific facts the historical record is sufficiently robust — Blackstone, colonial intoxication laws, and surety statutes collectively — that even a more rigorous originalist inquiry reaches the same destination. As Chief Justice, I will assign myself the majority opinion and write narrowly: the holding will be that Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied to habitual unlawful drug users whose pattern of use demonstrates persistent impairment of judgment, expressly reserving judgment on casual or occasional users and preserving as-applied challenges where the government cannot demonstrate the persistent danger the historical tradition targeted, consistent with Justice Kagan's and Justice Jackson's prudential concerns. This narrow framing should command a broad majority, protect institutional legitimacy by avoiding unnecessary constitutional pronouncements, and provide the authoritative circuit-conflict resolution that the deepening split across the Third, Fifth, and Seventh Circuits demands.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The conference has reached a unanimous position, and while I maintain my methodological concerns about Rahimi's analogical framework, I am persuaded that the historical record here is sufficiently robust to sustain the statute even under a more rigorous originalist inquiry. Justice Barrett's observation that Blackstone's commentaries, Founding-era surety laws, and colonial-era restrictions on the intoxicated and mentally impaired collectively reflect a genuine historical tradition of status-based disarmament tied to compromised judgment — not merely post-hoc rationalization — directly addresses my concern that the analogical methodology risks untethering analysis from original public meaning. I continue to resist Chief Justice Roberts's framing that the 'relevantly similar' standard should be applied loosely, and I would write separately to emphasize that the original public meaning of 'the people' in the Second Amendment was understood to exclude those whose persistent impairment of judgment rendered them incapable of responsible exercise of that right — grounding the holding in historical fact rather than analogical inference. The strongest argument for Respondent — that no Founding-era law precisely targeted habitual drug users as a disarmed class — is real but ultimately unavailing because the animating principle of the historical tradition, not merely its specific applications, is what the original public meaning inquiry demands.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The conference has reached a well-reasoned consensus, and I find Justice Thomas's methodological concern about Rahimi's analogical approach worth acknowledging even as I conclude it does not alter the outcome here — the historical record of Blackstone's commentaries, colonial-era intoxication laws, and surety statutes is sufficiently robust that even a more rigorous originalist inquiry yields the same result as the 'relevantly similar' standard. Justice Gorsuch's point about surety laws being status-based rather than requiring proof of active impairment at the moment of possession directly answers what I consider the strongest argument for Respondent: that 922(g)(3) sweeps too broadly by covering persons not actively intoxicated when possessing a firearm. I am persuaded by Chief Justice Roberts's suggestion that the opinion should be written narrowly — upholding the statute as applied to habitual unlawful drug users whose pattern of use demonstrates persistent impairment, while expressly reserving judgment on marginal applications — which both reflects sound textualist methodology and avoids the overreach that could invite future as-applied challenges to undermine the holding. Hemani's circumstances as a habitual user place him squarely within the historical tradition's core justification, and the deepening circuit conflict demands authoritative resolution on precisely these facts.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The conference has reached a genuinely persuasive convergence, and I find Justice Gorsuch's point about surety laws being status-based rather than requiring proof of active impairment at the moment of possession to be the most analytically decisive contribution — it directly neutralizes what I identified as the strongest argument for Respondent, namely that 922(g)(3) sweeps beyond the historical tradition by covering persons not actively intoxicated when possessing a firearm. Justice Barrett's methodological framing that the 'relevantly similar' inquiry asks about justification and burden — not a precise historical twin — is correct and consistent with Rahimi's explicit instruction, and the historical record of Blackstone's commentaries, surety laws, and colonial-era restrictions on the intoxicated and mentally impaired collectively reflects a genuine tradition of status-based disarmament tied to compromised judgment that maps onto habitual unlawful drug use. I maintain my view, shared with Justice Jackson and Justice Kagan, that the as-applied holding here must be written narrowly enough to preserve genuine as-applied challenges for casual or occasional users where the government cannot demonstrate the persistent, judgment-impairing condition that the historical tradition targeted — this is not merely a safety valve but a constitutional imperative given the real-world consequences for individuals whose drug use does not rise to the level of chronic impairment. The breadth concern is real, and I would write separately if the majority opinion does not expressly preserve that space.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The conference has reached a genuinely persuasive consensus, and I find Justice Gorsuch's point about surety laws being status-based rather than requiring proof of active impairment at the moment of possession to be the analytical linchpin that resolves the strongest argument for Respondent — namely, that Hemani was not actively intoxicated when he possessed the firearm. Justice Thomas raises a legitimate methodological concern about Rahimi's analogical approach potentially untethering analysis from original public meaning, but I think the historical record here is sufficiently robust that even under his more demanding standard, the tradition of disarming those with chronically compromised judgment sustains the statute as applied to habitual unlawful drug users. I remain committed to preserving as-applied challenges at the margins, consistent with Justice Sotomayor's and Justice Jackson's concerns about casual users, because the statute's breadth does present genuine constitutional questions that facial validity does not resolve — and a narrow holding that expressly reserves those questions is both more honest about the limits of our historical analysis and more consistent with good statutory construction. The facial invalidation by the Fifth Circuit was error, and I would reverse.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas's methodological concern about Rahimi's analogical approach remains the most intellectually serious challenge to my position, but I am persuaded that even under a rigorous originalist inquiry — one demanding fidelity to original public meaning rather than loose analogizing — the historical record here is sufficiently robust. As Justice Barrett correctly identifies, Blackstone's commentaries and Founding-era surety laws collectively reflect a genuine tradition of status-based disarmament tied to compromised judgment, not merely active impairment at a discrete moment, which means the historical foundation for upholding 922(g)(3) as applied to habitual users does not depend on Rahimi's more flexible methodology alone. I share Justice Kagan's and Justice Jackson's concern about the statute's breadth at the margins — a casual or occasional user presents a genuinely harder case where the historical tradition's animating principle may not map cleanly — and I would write to preserve robust as-applied challenges rather than treating today's holding as foreclosing them. Hemani's circumstances as a habitual unlawful user place him squarely within the historical tradition's core, and the Fifth Circuit's demand for a precise historical twin was error under any defensible reading of Rahimi.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable degree of convergence, and I find the collective reasoning has actually strengthened rather than weakened my position. Justice Thomas raises the most intellectually honest methodological concern — that Rahimi's analogical approach risks untethering Second Amendment analysis from original public meaning — but I think the historical record here is sufficiently robust that even under his more rigorous originalist inquiry, the tradition of disarming those of 'unsound mind' and the chronically intoxicated reflects a genuine Founding-era principle of status-based disarmament tied to compromised judgment, not merely a loose analogy. Justice Gorsuch's point about surety laws being status-based rather than requiring proof of active impairment at the moment of possession remains the most persuasive answer to the respondent's strongest argument, and I would write narrowly — upholding the statute as applied to habitual unlawful users like Hemani while expressly preserving as-applied challenges for marginal cases, consistent with Justice Kagan's and Justice Jackson's legitimate concerns about the statute's breadth at the margins. The institutional imperative of resolving the deepening circuit conflict, combined with Rahimi's clear instruction that 'relevantly similar' rather than 'historical twin' is the governing standard, confirms my vote for the Petitioner.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The conference has reached a well-reasoned consensus, and the collective deliberation has actually strengthened rather than weakened my position. Justice Thomas's methodological concern — that Rahimi's analogical approach risks untethering analysis from original public meaning — remains the most intellectually serious challenge, but as I noted in my initial reasoning, the historical record here is robust enough to satisfy even a more rigorous originalist inquiry: Blackstone's treatment of dangerous persons, colonial-era disarmament of the intoxicated, and surety laws collectively reflect a genuine Founding-era tradition of status-based disarmament tied to compromised judgment, not merely post-hoc rationalization. Justice Gorsuch correctly identifies that Rahimi's endorsement of surety laws — which addressed probabilistic, recurring danger rather than requiring proof of active impairment at a single moment — directly refutes the Fifth Circuit's demand for a precise historical twin and maps onto habitual drug use more comfortably than the court below acknowledged. I write to emphasize, consistent with Justice Kagan's framing, that today's holding is an as-applied determination: the facial validity of 922(g)(3) as applied to habitual unlawful drug users like Hemani does not foreclose future as-applied challenges where the government cannot demonstrate the persistent, judgment-impairing condition that the historical tradition was designed to address.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The conference has reached a genuinely well-reasoned consensus, and deliberation has only strengthened my position. Justice Thomas raises the most intellectually honest challenge — that Rahimi's analogical methodology risks untethering Second Amendment analysis from original public meaning — but I find that even under his more rigorous originalist framework, the historical record of disarming intoxicated persons and those of 'unsound mind' reflects a genuine Founding-era tradition of categorical disarmament based on compromised judgment that maps onto habitual unlawful drug use. The strongest argument for Respondent remains that 922(g)(3) targets a status-based condition rather than acute impairment, but as Justice Gorsuch correctly notes, Rahimi's endorsement of surety laws — which addressed probabilistic, recurring danger rather than imminent active threat — forecloses the Fifth Circuit's demand for proof of active intoxication at the moment of possession. My public defender background still compels me to insist that the majority opinion expressly preserve robust as-applied challenges for casual or occasional users, consistent with Justice Kagan's and Justice Sotomayor's shared concern, because the breadth of 922(g)(3) at the margins remains a genuine constitutional vulnerability that a narrow holding can and should acknowledge.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Rahimi's clarification of the Bruen framework, the historical-tradition inquiry does not require a precise historical twin but rather a 'relevantly similar' analogue grounded in comparable principles — here, the longstanding tradition of disarming persons whose judgment or self-control is compromised by intoxicants or mental impairment provides sufficient analogical support for Section 922(g)(3). The deep circuit conflict between the Fifth Circuit's invalidation and the Third and Seventh Circuits' contrary holdings itself signals that the statute is not obviously unconstitutional, and institutional legitimacy counsels against striking down a federal public safety statute absent a clear historical record demanding that result. Writing narrowly, I would hold only that the statute survives as-applied to habitual unlawful drug users whose pattern of use demonstrates the kind of persistent impairment of judgment that historical disarmament traditions targeted, without resolving every conceivable application of the statute. The Court's obligation to resolve the circuit conflict, combined with Rahimi's endorsement of principle-based rather than law-specific analogical reasoning, tips the balance toward upholding the statute on these facts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: While I have serious reservations about the Bruen framework's application as elaborated in Rahimi — which I believe insufficiently anchors Second Amendment analysis in the original public meaning of the text and relies too heavily on malleable historical analogizing — the historical record does support a tradition of disarming individuals whose judgment and faculties are compromised by intoxicants, as reflected in Founding-era laws and Blackstone's commentaries on dangerous persons. Section 922(g)(3), properly understood, targets individuals whose habitual unlawful drug use creates a category of persons whose impaired judgment renders them dangerous in a manner analogous to historical disarmament of the intoxicated and mentally ill. I would uphold the statute as applied here, though I write separately to emphasize that the correct constitutional inquiry must be grounded in the original public meaning of 'the right of the people to keep and bear Arms' and the historical understanding of who constituted 'the people' entitled to that right, rather than the freewheeling analogical reasoning Rahimi permits. The circuit conflict created by the Fifth Circuit's ruling below, now deepened by the Third Circuit in Harris, demands this Court's resolution to restore uniformity in a domain touching fundamental constitutional rights.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutionally valid under the Bruen historical-tradition framework because Rahimi confirmed that the Second Amendment permits categorical disarmament of individuals who pose a demonstrated danger to public safety, and habitual unlawful drug users — by definition engaging in ongoing criminal conduct that impairs judgment — fall within that tradition. The historical analogues need not be a perfect mirror; as Rahimi clarified, courts must identify laws that are 'relevantly similar' in justification and burden, and the longstanding tradition of disarming intoxicated persons, combined with laws targeting the mentally ill and those of 'unsound mind,' provides sufficient analogical support for a statute targeting persons whose habitual illegal drug use creates a persistent condition of impaired judgment and heightened danger. The Fifth Circuit's cramped reading — demanding a precise historical twin rather than a 'relevantly similar' analogue — misreads Rahimi's methodology and would effectively immunize a dangerous class of persons from a commonsense public safety regulation. Practical consequences reinforce this reading: invalidating 922(g)(3) would gut hundreds of federal prosecutions annually and eliminate a critical law enforcement tool targeting individuals whose criminal drug use and firearm possession create compounding public safety risks.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: While I have deep reservations about Bruen's rigid historical-tradition framework — reservations I expressed in my Rahimi concurrence — the methodology the Court established in Rahimi provides sufficient analytical tools to uphold Section 922(g)(3) as applied here. Rahimi confirmed that historical analogues need not be 'twins' but must be 'relevantly similar' in their 'why' and 'how,' and the historical tradition of disarming intoxicated persons, combined with Founding-era laws targeting those deemed to pose heightened dangers to public safety, provides a sufficiently analogous basis for disarming habitual unlawful drug users whose chronic impairment creates ongoing public safety risks. The practical stakes matter enormously: striking down 922(g)(3) would gut hundreds of federal prosecutions annually and eliminate a critical tool for keeping firearms from individuals whose judgment and impulse control are chronically compromised by substance dependence, disproportionately harming the very vulnerable communities I am committed to protecting. The circuit conflict — now deepened by the Third Circuit in Harris — demands resolution, and the government's historical analogues, though imperfect, are sufficient under the flexible Rahimi standard to sustain the statute's constitutionality at least as applied to a habitual user like Hemani.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Rahimi's clarification of Bruen, the historical-tradition inquiry does not require a 'dead ringer' analogue but rather asks whether the modern regulation is 'relevantly similar' to historical laws in both 'why' and 'how' — and here, the historical tradition of disarming intoxicated persons and those deemed dangerously impaired provides a sufficiently analogous regulatory principle supporting Section 922(g)(3). The statute's categorical approach mirrors Congress's longstanding authority, recognized in Heller itself, to disarm persons who pose heightened public safety risks due to compromised judgment and impulse control, a principle that extends naturally from intoxication-based laws to habitual unlawful drug use. While I share some concern about the statute's breadth as applied to individuals not actively impaired at the moment of possession — a concern that might warrant as-applied relief in narrow circumstances — the Fifth Circuit's wholesale invalidation of most applications of 922(g)(3) goes too far and creates an unworkable circuit conflict that undermines hundreds of legitimate federal prosecutions annually. The more administrable and textually coherent approach is to uphold the statute on its face while leaving room for genuine as-applied challenges where the government cannot demonstrate the defendant posed the kind of heightened danger the historical tradition was designed to address.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under Bruen's historical-tradition framework as clarified by Rahimi, the government need not produce a precise historical twin but rather a 'well-established and representative historical analogue' that is relevantly similar in justification and burden. Rahimi demonstrated that surety laws and 'going armed' statutes — which disarmed individuals who posed a probabilistic, recurring danger to others, not merely those imminently dangerous at the precise moment of an encounter — are sufficient analogues, suggesting the Court endorses status-based disarmament tied to demonstrated dangerousness rather than requiring proof of active impairment at the moment of possession. Historical laws disarming intoxicated persons, the mentally ill, and those adjudged dangerous collectively reflect a tradition of disarming individuals whose judgment and self-control are compromised in ways that make firearm possession categorically more dangerous, and habitual unlawful drug users fit within that tradition's animating principle. The Fifth Circuit's narrow reading — requiring proof of active intoxication at the moment of possession — is inconsistent with Rahimi's more flexible analogical methodology and creates an unworkable standard that the historical record does not compel.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Rahimi's methodology, the historical-tradition test does not require a 'historical twin' but rather a 'relevantly similar' analogue that shares comparable justification and burden — and the historical record of disarming intoxicated persons and those deemed mentally unfit for responsible firearm use provides sufficient analogical support for Section 922(g)(3). As I emphasized in my Rahimi concurrence, Heller itself identified 'presumptively lawful' regulatory measures and recognized that the Second Amendment permits disarming those who are not 'law-abiding, responsible citizens,' a category that reasonably encompasses habitual unlawful drug users whose ongoing illegal conduct and impaired judgment create heightened public safety risks. The practical workability concerns are also significant here — the Fifth Circuit's ruling threatens hundreds of federal prosecutions annually and has created a deepening circuit conflict with the Third and Seventh Circuits that demands resolution in favor of a workable, historically grounded standard. While I acknowledge the statute's breadth raises legitimate as-applied concerns at the margins, the core application to habitual unlawful drug users is constitutionally defensible under the analogical reasoning Rahimi endorsed.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying the Bruen/Rahimi framework with appropriate methodological rigor, the historical tradition supports disarming individuals who pose heightened dangers due to mental or physical impairment, and habitual unlawful drug users fall within that tradition's principles even if no precise historical twin exists. As Rahimi clarified, the inquiry is whether the modern regulation is 'relevantly similar' to historical analogues in both justification and burden — not whether a founding-era law addressed the identical circumstance. Historical laws disarming the intoxicated, the mentally ill, and those deemed dangerous to public order share the same underlying principle as Section 922(g)(3): that individuals whose judgment and self-control are chronically compromised by substance use present an elevated risk when armed. While I acknowledge the statute's breadth raises legitimate as-applied concerns at the margins, the government has met its burden under Rahimi's more flexible analogical reasoning to sustain the statute's constitutionality in the general case, and the deepening circuit conflict — now spanning the Third, Fifth, and Seventh Circuits — demands this Court provide authoritative resolution consistent with Heller's recognition that the Second Amendment is not unlimited.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under the Rahimi framework, the government need not identify a precise historical twin but must demonstrate that Section 922(g)(3) is 'relevantly similar' to historical regulations in both 'why' and 'how' — and the historical tradition of disarming intoxicated persons and those deemed dangerously impaired satisfies this standard when extended to habitual unlawful drug users, who present an analogous category of persons whose judgment and impulse control are chronically compromised. Rahimi confirmed that Bruen permits categorical disarmament of persons who pose a demonstrated heightened danger to public safety, and habitual drug users — whose ongoing unlawful substance use creates persistent conditions of impaired judgment — fall within that principle even if they are not actively intoxicated at the precise moment of possession. My background as a public defender gives me genuine concern about the statute's breadth and vagueness as applied to casual or occasional users, and I would signal that as-applied challenges in cases involving minimal or remote drug use deserve serious consideration, but Hemani's circumstances as an unlawful user bring him within the core of what the historical tradition supports. The circuit conflict identified in Harris and the Fifth Circuit's ruling below demands resolution, and the practical consequences of invalidating hundreds of prosecutions annually — combined with Rahimi's instruction that historical analogues need only share a comparable justification and burden — tips the balance toward upholding the statute in this as-applied challenge.
